extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political theory, constitutional law, and comparative politics
extracted.subtask_description: Analytical chapter on the effects of elective executive power and the design, necessity, and jurisdiction of a federal judiciary in the United States. Discusses mode of presidential election (electoral college), crises around elections and re‑eligibility, and reasons for creating federal courts and a Supreme Court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dangers of the elective system for the head of state
rubrics_metrics.description: The elective system introduces instability into internal and external policy because the head of state’s power is temporary, limited, and subordinate; approaching elections suspend executive action and induce distraction and indifference in office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that candidates cannot marshal long‑term power or patronage to build durable factions; during election periods the incumbent often suspends major initiatives (example: Jefferson’s remark in 1809). Translator’s note cites Buchanan’s post‑election paralysis (Nov 1860–Mar 1861) as enabling secession. The danger is moderated when executive power is small and circumscribed (as in the U.S.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantage of hereditary monarchies: continuity of executive action
rubrics_metrics.description: Hereditary monarchy ties private family interest to state interest, ensuring executive government is never suspended and there is always someone to conduct affairs, for better or worse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts with elective states where government ‘wheels’ may cease at election time; hereditary systems provide continuity even if not superior in conduct. Use this as a comparative criterion when assessing systems' stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electoral college (special electoral body) as chosen mode of election
rubrics_metrics.description: Delegating choice to a body of special electors (rather than the legislature or direct popular vote) was adopted to express the people’s choice with minimal excitement and suspense and to make a majority more probable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning: fewer electors increase chance of decision and allow a judicious, timely choice; electors vote separately (same day) and transmit sealed lists to the President of the Senate; if no majority, the House chooses among the top three — this design balances respect for popular voice with rapid execution and safeguards against corruption and prolonged uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural rules for electors and contingency resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Electors from each state vote on the same day and transmit sealed votes; if no candidate has a majority of electoral votes, the House of Representatives elects the President from the three highest vote‑getters, with each state delegation casting one vote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes advantages of simultaneous voting and sealed transmission to limit intrigue; highlights that the House decision is rare but may still be indecisive (no constitutional remedy if House majority is unclear). Footnotes explain elector counts and state‑based voting weight; historical examples (Jefferson 1801, Quincy Adams 1825).

rubrics_metrics.name: Election as a national crisis and its political dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: The period of a presidential election is a national crisis because collective interest inflames passions, divides citizens into partisan camps, and absorbs public attention and government energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes effects: increased factional ardor, President absorbed with self‑defense/re‑election, public papers and conversation dominated by election, and subsequent calming after decision. Translator notes exception: Lincoln’s election precipitated civil war. Use to evaluate election‑period risks to governance and social order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re‑eligibility (re‑election) of the President undermines independence and increases corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowing re‑election encourages the use of state resources for personal electoral advantage, makes the incumbent subordinate to popular caprice, and transforms governance into electioneering, thereby extending the natural vices of elective government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument balances pros (retain proven talent in crisis) versus cons (incumbent borrows state power for campaign, places personal re‑election above public good). Concludes that re‑eligibility partly destroys the intended independence of the executive and increases daily dangers to the republic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited executive power in the U.S. reduces danger from elective system
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the President’s constitutional powers are relatively small and circumscribed in the U.S., slackening of government action during elections is less dangerous than it would be where the executive is strong; weak executive limits damage from suspension of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains American circumstances (vast territory, few hostile neighbors, dispersed population) that make elections less perilous; compares with European nations where a powerful executive’s suspension could be catastrophic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of a federal judiciary to enforce Union laws
rubrics_metrics.description: A federal government especially needs judicial institutions because moral force (courts' authority) substitutes for physical force and enables the Union to enforce obedience to federal laws without resort to violence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that without courts a government would rely on physical force or tolerate insubordination, risking anarchy or despotism; federal courts provide a legal barrier between government power and use of force and are essential for a weak but lawful central government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal courts must be established rather than relying solely on state tribunals
rubrics_metrics.description: The Union could not entrust execution of federal laws to state courts because state tribunals are politically 'foreign' and partial; allowing them to decide federal matters would undermine national sovereignty and lead to divergent interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that states have distinct origins, maxims, and interests; state judges would be partial; entrusting federal law enforcement to state courts risks inconsistent and partial justice. Therefore, national courts were created to secure impartial application of Union laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization and independence of the national judiciary
rubrics_metrics.description: The national judiciary consists of a Supreme Court with inferior courts appended; Supreme Court justices are appointed by the President with Senate advice, hold inalienable office (life tenure), and have protected salaries to ensure independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details: district courts for local causes, circuit courts for more important cases, Supreme Court for the gravest cases; life tenure and salary protection prevent influence by other authorities and preserve impartiality. Citations to practice and legislation (Organic Law of Sept. 24, 1789) support the arrangement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme Court as arbiter of jurisdictional conflicts and source of uniform jurisprudence
rubrics_metrics.description: Because no neutral external arbiter exists between federal and state superior courts, the Supreme Court of the United States is invested with the right to determine questions of jurisdiction to ensure a uniform interpretation of Union laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: giving this power to state courts would de facto destroy federal supremacy; central judicial determination creates a uniform body of jurisprudence. Acknowledges the blow to state independence but argues the practical danger is limited by relative federal weakness and judicial prudence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number and diversity of state tribunals make them unfit to interpret federal law uniformly
rubrics_metrics.description: The multiplicity (then 13, later 24) and divergent interpretations of state courts rendered them unsuitable for administering federal law because they would produce conflicting constructions of fundamental law across the Union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that a nation cannot subsist when foundational laws are subject to numerous different interpretations; consolidating judicial power at the federal level avoids legal fragmentation and preserves coherence of Union law.
